title: Trump Administration Revokes 28,000 Immigrant Trucker Licences in Crackdown
excerpt: The mass cancellation of commercial driving licences targets undocumented immigrants and tightens rules that could affect Indian-origin truckers in the United States.
body:
• The Trump administration has cancelled over 28,000 commercial driver's licences it says were illegally issued to undocumented immigrants, and revoked 24,000 more for failing English-language proficiency requirements
  • Under new rules, commercial licences will be available only to immigrants holding valid H-2A, H-2B or E-2 visas, significantly narrowing eligibility
  • Immigrants make up roughly 20 percent of the US trucking workforce, and the administration has launched a 'Freedom Haul' programme to replace affected drivers with military veterans

The Trump administration has cancelled the commercial driver's licences of more than 28,000 undocumented immigrants, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt confirmed, in one of the most sweeping enforcement actions targeting the US trucking industry. The crackdown, which also shuttered 9,500 driving schools, has direct implications for Indian-origin truckers in the United States.

The administration said it had coordinated with state authorities to revoke what it described as "illegally issued" commercial licences and shut down driving schools that it alleged had helped unqualified drivers obtain credentials. Separately, officials worked with states to cancel approximately 24,000 additional commercial licences held by non-citizens who did not meet English-language proficiency requirements.

Tighter Rules, Narrower Eligibility

Under the new framework, commercial driver's licences will be available only to immigrants holding valid H-2A visas (temporary agricultural workers), H-2B visas (temporary non-agricultural workers) or E-2 visas (treaty investors). The restriction effectively bars most immigrant truckers from holding commercial licences unless they fall within these narrow visa categories.

https://x.com/CNNnews18/status/2084827765786964086

The US Department of Transportation began enforcing existing English-language proficiency requirements for commercial truck drivers last summer. The administration said audits across all 50 states found numerous commercial licences held by non-domiciled immigrants that remained valid after work permits had expired or had been issued without proper immigration status verification.

The Florida Crash That Fuelled the Crackdown

The enforcement push gained momentum following a fatal crash in Florida in August, when a truck driver allegedly made an illegal U-turn, killing three people. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the Indian-origin driver involved should not have been issued a commercial driver's licence.

"We are removing more and more dangerous foreign drivers off our roads every day and restoring the integrity of America's trucking industry."

— Sean Duffy, US Transportation Secretary

The administration subsequently announced the "Freedom Haul" initiative, aimed at replacing affected immigrant truck drivers with US military veterans. Duffy said the programme would make it easier for former service members to "get behind the wheel of a big rig."

Funding Fights With States

The federal government has sought to withhold millions of dollars in highway funding from California and New York, accusing the two states of failing to revoke additional licences. The funding dispute is now before the courts. Pennsylvania, Minnesota and North Carolina have also been warned they could lose federal highway funding if they fail to comply with the administration's directives.

What It Means for Indians in the US

According to administration figures, immigrants account for roughly 20 percent of the US trucking workforce. Non-domiciled commercial licences issued to immigrants represent about 5 percent of all commercial licences, covering approximately 200,000 drivers.

For the Indian community in the United States, the implications are significant. Indian-origin drivers make up a visible share of the immigrant trucking workforce, and the new restrictions could affect those whose visa status does not fall within the three permitted categories. The policy also signals the administration's broader posture toward immigrant labour in industries where foreign-born workers have traditionally filled critical gaps.

The combination of licence revocations, tighter eligibility rules and the veteran replacement programme marks one of the most aggressive interventions in the US commercial transport sector in recent years, with ripple effects likely to extend well beyond the trucking industry.
